Genesis — Book introduction

The name Genesis comes from Greek and means “the book of generation or production.”

It is a fitting name, because the book tells us how all things began.

No other history reaches so far back.

Nothing in the most ancient surviving book contradicts its account. Indeed, much that we find in the writings of the earliest pagan authors, or in the customs of different nations, confirms what Genesis tells us.

God creates heaven and earth (verses 1–2)

The Bible's opening verse gives us a satisfying and useful account of how heaven and earth began.

Humble Christians understand this by faith better than the most learned people's speculations can explain it. Looking at heaven and earth, we see the power of their great Creator.

Our own nature and place in creation should remind us of our duty. As Christians, we must always keep heaven before our eyes and the earth beneath our feet.

The Son of God, who is one with the Father, was with him when he made the world. More than that, Scripture repeatedly tells us that the world was made by the Son, and that nothing was made without him.

What high thoughts we should have of the great God we worship, and of the great Mediator in whose name we pray!

Here, at the very beginning of Scripture, we also meet the Holy Spirit, whose work in human hearts is described so often throughout the Bible.

At first the world had nothing pleasing to see. It was without form and empty, full of confusion and darkness.

God's work of grace in a person's soul is also a new creation.

A soul without grace, not yet born again, is disordered and confused, filled with every kind of evil. It is empty of all that is good because it is without God. It is dark—indeed, darkness itself.

That is our natural condition until almighty grace changes us.

The creation of light (verses 3–5)

God said, “Let there be light.” He willed it, and light appeared at once.

What power there is in God's word!

In the new creation of the soul, light comes first too. The blessed Spirit enlightens our understanding, and through that enlightenment works upon our will and affections.

People who were darkness because of sin become light in the Lord through grace.

Without the coming of the Son of God to give us understanding, fallen humanity would have remained in darkness forever (1 John 5:20).

God approved the light he had called into being. He also separated it from darkness.

What fellowship can light have with darkness?

In heaven there is perfect light, without any darkness. In hell there is complete darkness, without a glimmer of light.

Day and night both belong to the Lord. Let us use them both for his honor: working for him each day, resting in him each night, and meditating on his law both day and night.

God separates the earth from the waters and makes it fruitful (verses 6–13)

The earth was empty. But God spoke, and it was filled with his riches. They still belong to him.

He allows us to use them, but they come from God and should be used in his service and for his honor.

At his command, the earth produces grass, plants and fruit.

We should give God the glory for every benefit we receive from what the earth produces.

If, through grace, we have a share in him who is the Fountain, we can still rejoice in him when the streams of earthly mercy run dry.

God makes the sun, moon and stars (verses 14–19)

On the fourth day, God made the sun, moon and stars. All are his works.

Scripture speaks of the stars as they appear to our eyes. It does not tell us their number, nature, location, size or movements.

The Bible was not written to satisfy our curiosity or turn us into astronomers. It was written to lead us to God and make us holy.

The lights of heaven serve their Creator faithfully. They shine in their appointed seasons without fail.

We too have been set as lights in the world to serve God. But do we fulfill the purpose for which we were created as faithfully as they do?

We do not.

Our light does not shine before God as his lights shine before us. We burn our Master's candles but neglect our Master's work.

God creates living creatures (verses 20–25)

God commanded fish and birds to come into being, and he himself carried out that command.

Insects are more numerous than birds and beasts, and just as remarkable. They seem to have been included in this day's work.

The Creator's wisdom and power are no less wonderful in an ant than in an elephant.

God's providence preserves everything he has made, and every creature's fruitfulness comes from his blessing.

God makes humanity in his image (verses 26–28)

Human beings were made last. This was both an honor and a kindness to them.

Yet they were created on the same day as the animals. Their bodies were formed from the same earth, and while they live in those bodies, they share that earth with the animals.

God forbid that by indulging our bodily desires we should become like the beasts that perish!

Human beings were made different from everything that came before. In them, flesh and spirit—earth and heaven—were brought together.

God said, “Let us make man.”

When humanity was created, it was meant to glorify the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

We are baptized into that great name, and we owe our very existence to the One whose name it is.

It is especially the human soul that bears God's image.

Humanity was created upright (Ecclesiastes 7:29). The mind understood divine things clearly and truly, without error or misunderstanding.

The will agreed immediately and entirely with God's will.

Every affection was rightly ordered. There were no sinful appetites or uncontrolled passions. Thoughts could readily settle upon what was best.

How holy and happy our first parents were when they bore God's image!

And how terribly that image has been defaced in humanity.

May the Lord renew it in our souls by his grace!

God appoints food (verses 29–30)

God gave people plants and fruit for food, including grain and all the produce of the earth.

Let God's people entrust their needs to him. They need not be consumed by worry over what they will eat or drink.

The God who feeds his birds will not let his little children starve.

God approves the completed creation (verse 31)

When we examine our own work, we discover with shame that much of it has been very bad.

But when God looked upon everything he had made, it was all very good.

It was good because everything was exactly as its Creator intended.

All God's works, throughout his dominion, bless him. So let my soul bless the Lord!

Let us thank God for the gospel of Christ. And as we think about his almighty power, let us, as sinners, flee from the wrath to come.

If we are created anew in God's image, in holiness, we will one day enter the “new heavens and new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.”

Verses 1-2
The first verse of the Bible gives us a satisfying and useful account of the origin of the earth and the heavens. The faith of humble Christians understands this better than the fancy of the most learned men. From what we see of heaven and earth, we learn the power of the great Creator. And let our make and place as men, remind us of our duty as Christians, always to keep heaven in our eye, and the earth under our feet. The Son of God, one with the Father, was with him when he made the world; nay, we are often told that the world was made by him, and nothing was made without him. Oh, what high thoughts should there be in our minds, of that great God whom we worship, and of that great Mediator in whose name we pray! And here, at the beginning of the sacred volume, we read of that Divine Spirit, whose work upon the heart of man is so often mentioned in other parts of the Bible. Observe, that at first there was nothing desirable to be seen, for the world was without form, and void; it was confusion, and emptiness. In like manner the work of grace in the soul is a new creation: and in a graceless soul, one that is not born again, there is disorder, confusion, and every evil work: it is empty of all good, for it is without God; it is dark, it is darkness itself: this is our condition by nature, till Almighty grace works a change in us.
[Gen.1.3-Gen.1.5]
Verses 3-5
God said, Let there be light; he willed it, and at once there was light. Oh, the power of the word of God! And in the new creation, the first thing that is wrought in the soul is light: the blessed Spirit works upon the will and affections by enlightening the understanding. Those who by sin were darkness, by grace become light in the Lord. Darkness would have been always upon fallen man, if the Son of God had not come and given us understanding, [1John.5.20] 1Jo 5:20. The light which God willed, he approved of. God divided the light from the darkness; for what fellowship has light with darkness? In heaven there is perfect light, and no darkness at all; in hell, utter darkness, and no gleam of light. The day and the night are the Lord's; let us use both to his honour, by working for him every day, and resting in him every night, meditating in his law both day and night.
[Gen.1.6-Gen.1.13]
Verses 6-13
The earth was emptiness, but by a word spoken, it became full of God's riches, and his they are still. Though the use of them is allowed to man, they are from God, and to his service and honour they must be used. The earth, at his command, brings forth grass, herbs, and fruits. God must have the glory of all the benefit we receive from the produce of the earth. If we have, through grace, an interest in Him who is the Fountain, we may rejoice in him when the streams of temporal mercies are dried up.
[Gen.1.14-Gen.1.19]
Verses 14-19
In the fourth day's work, the creation of the sun, moon, and stars is accounted for. All these are the works of God. The stars are spoken of as they appear to our eyes, without telling their number, nature, place, size, or motions; for the Scriptures were written, not to gratify curiosity, or make us astronomers, but to lead us to God, and make us saints. The lights of heaven are made to serve him; they do it faithfully, and shine in their season without fail. We are set as lights in this world to serve God; but do we in like manner answer the end of our creation? We do not: our light does not shine before God, as his lights shine before us. We burn our Master's candles, but do not mind our Master's work.
[Gen.1.20-Gen.1.25]
Verses 20-25
God commanded the fish and fowl to be produced. This command he himself executed. Insects, which are more numerous than the birds and beasts, and as curious, seem to have been part of this day's work. The Creator's wisdom and power are to be admired as much in an ant as in an elephant. The power of God's providence preserves all things, and fruitfulness is the effect of his blessing.
[Gen.1.26-Gen.1.28]
Verses 26-28
Man was made last of all the creatures: this was both an honour and a favour to him. Yet man was made the same day that the beasts were; his body was made of the same earth with theirs; and while he is in the body, he inhabits the same earth with them. God forbid that by indulging the body, and the desires of it, we should make ourselves like the beasts that perish! Man was to be a creature different from all that had been hitherto made. Flesh and spirit, heaven and earth, must be put together in him. God said, "Let us make man." Man, when he was made, was to glorify the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Into that great name we are baptized, for to that great name we owe our being. It is the soul of man that especially bears God's image. Man was made upright, [Eccl.7.29] Ec 7:29. His understanding saw Divine things clearly and truly; there were no errors or mistakes in his knowledge; his will consented at once, and in all things, to the will of God. His affections were all regular, and he had no bad appetites or passions. His thoughts were easily brought and fixed to the best subjects. Thus holy, thus happy, were our first parents in having the image of God upon them. But how is this image of God upon man defaced! May the Lord renew it upon our souls by his grace!
[Gen.1.29-Gen.1.30]
Verses 29-30
Herbs and fruits must be man's food, including corn, and all the products of the earth. Let God's people cast their care upon him, and not be troubled about what they shall eat, and what they shall drink. He that feeds his birds will not starve his babes.
[Gen.1.31]
Verse 31
When we come to think about our works, we find, to our shame, that much has been very bad; but when God saw his work, all was very good. Good, for it was all just as the Creator would have it to be. All his works, in all places of his dominion, bless him; and therefore, bless thou the Lord, O my soul. Let us bless God for the gospel of Christ, and when we consider his almighty power, let us sinners flee from the wrath to come. If new--created unto the image of God in holiness, we shall at length enter the "new heavens and new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness."

The first Sabbath (verses 1–3)

After six days, God ceased his work of creation. In miracles, he has overridden nature, but he has never changed its established course or added to it.

God did not rest because he was tired. He rested because he was pleased with what he had made.

Here we see the beginning of the kingdom of grace, in God's setting apart the Sabbath as holy.

Everyone to whom God has made his holy Sabbaths known has a duty to observe one day in seven solemnly, as a day of holy rest and holy work for his honor.

At that time, no human beings existed except our first parents. The Sabbath was appointed for them, and clearly for all the generations that would follow.

The Christian Sabbath we observe is one day in seven. On it we celebrate the rest of God the Son and the completion of the work of our redemption.

The Creator, the earth, and the human soul (verses 4–7)

Here the Creator is given the name “Jehovah.” Wherever our English Bibles print “LORD” in capital letters, the original uses “Jehovah.”

This name declares that God alone exists of himself, and that he gives existence to every creature and everything else.

Plants and herbs receive special attention because God made them and appointed them as food for humanity.

The earth did not produce its fruit by itself. It did so through almighty power.

In the same way, grace does not grow by itself in the natural soil of the human soul. It is God's work.

Rain, too, is God's gift. It did not come until the Lord God caused it to fall.

God ordinarily works through means, yet he can do his work without them whenever he chooses.

We must not put God to the test by neglecting the means he has given us. But we must trust him both when those means are available and when they are not.

In one way or another, God will water what he himself has planted.

Divine grace falls like dew and waters the church quietly.

God formed the human body from the fine dust on the surface of the earth.

But the soul was not made from the earth as the body was. How sad, then, that it should cling to the earth and devote itself to earthly things!

Before long, we must give God an account of how we have used our souls.

If we lose our souls, even though we gain the whole world, we are ruined forever.

Fools despise their own souls by caring more for their bodies.

The garden of Eden and its two trees (verses 8–14)

God did not give Adam a palace to live in, but a garden.

The more content we are with simple things, and the less we seek what feeds pride and luxury, the closer we come to innocence.

Nature is content with a little and with what is most natural. Grace is content with even less. But sinful desire craves everything and is never satisfied.

Nothing can truly satisfy the soul except the delights God himself has provided and appointed for it.

Eden means delight and pleasure.

Wherever the garden was, it had every desirable convenience without a single disadvantage. No other house or garden on earth has ever been like it.

It was beautiful with trees pleasing to the eye and rich with trees whose fruit was delicious and good for food.

Like a tender Father, God cared not only for Adam's benefit but also for his pleasure. Innocence brings pleasure—indeed, only in innocence is there true pleasure.

When Providence places us amid abundance and delight, we ought to serve God joyfully with the good things he has given us.

Two trees were unique to Eden.

First, the tree of life stood in the middle of the garden. Adam could eat from it and live.

Christ is now the Tree of Life to us (Revelation 2:7; 22:2), and the Bread of Life (John 6:48, 51).

Second, there was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

It bore this name because God had given a definite revelation of his will concerning it. Through that command, Adam could know moral good and evil.

What was good? Not eating from that tree. What was evil? Eating from it.

Through these two trees, God placed before Adam good and evil, blessing and curse.

Adam is placed in the garden to work (verse 15)

After making Adam, God placed him in the garden. This left no room for boasting.

Only the One who made us can make us happy.

He formed our bodies and is the Father of our spirits. No one else can fully provide for the happiness of both.

Even in Paradise, human beings had work to do. None of us was sent into the world to be idle.

The God who gave us bodies and souls has also given us abilities with which to work. And the God who gave us the earth as our home has given us tasks to carry out upon it.

Even the children and heirs of heaven must spend some of their time and thought on earthly responsibilities while they live here.

When they do this work with their eyes on God, they serve him just as truly as when they kneel in prayer.

Farming is an ancient and honorable calling. It was needed even in Paradise.

There is also real pleasure in doing the work God has called us to do.

Adam could not have been happy in idleness. God's law still stands: anyone unwilling to work has no right to eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

God's command and the trial of obedience (verses 16–17)

Let us never set our own will against God's holy will.

Adam was free to eat the fruits of Paradise. More than that, everlasting life was assured to him on condition of obedience.

God appointed a test of his obedience.

By transgressing the command, Adam would forfeit his Maker's favor and deserve his displeasure, with all its dreadful consequences: pain, disease, and death.

Worse still, he would lose God's holy image and the comfort of his favor.

He would suffer the torment of sinful passions and the terror of his Maker's vengeance, enduring forever with his undying soul.

The prohibition against eating the fruit of one particular tree was wisely suited to the condition of our first parents.

While innocent and alone in the world, what opportunity or temptation did they have to break any of the Ten Commandments?

What happened afterward shows that the whole human race was involved in the trial and fall of our first parents.

To argue against this is to struggle both against stubborn facts and against divine revelation.

Human beings are sinful. From their earliest actions, and throughout their lives, they show how ready they are to do evil.

They remain under God's displeasure, exposed to suffering and death.

Scripture consistently describes humanity as sinful and miserable in this way. These truths apply to people of every age and every nation.

The animals, the woman, and marriage (verses 18–25)

God gave Adam authority over the creatures. As proof of that authority, Adam named them all.

Giving them names also demonstrated his understanding of God's works.

Yet although he was lord over the creatures, nothing in the created world was a suitable helper for him.

Every helper we have comes from God. If we rest in him, he will work all things for good.

God caused Adam to fall into a deep sleep. While Adam knew no sin, God ensured that he would feel no pain.

Then God, like a father bringing his daughter to her husband, brought the woman to Adam as his second self and a helper suited to him.

A wife whom God has especially prepared by his grace and brought by his providence is likely to become a fitting helper to her husband.

How much wisdom and prayer we need when choosing a relationship so close and lasting!

Something that is meant to last a lifetime must be entered into carefully.

Our first parents needed no clothes to protect them from cold or heat, because neither could harm them. Nor did they need clothing for decoration.

How easy and happy life was for humanity in its innocence!

How good God had been to Adam! How many favors he had given him! How simple were the laws he had commanded him to keep!

Yet humanity, though placed in such honor, failed to understand what was truly in its own interest, and soon became like the beasts that perish.

The serpent deceives Eve (verses 1–5)

Satan attacked our first parents to draw them into sin, and the temptation proved disastrous.

The tempter was the devil, appearing in the form of a serpent. His aim was to lead Adam and Eve into sin and separate them from God.

From the beginning, then, the devil was a murderer and a great troublemaker.

He approached the woman when she was alone. That was part of his strategy.

Being alone gives many temptations a special advantage. Fellowship with other believers, on the other hand, greatly strengthens and protects us.

Satan also took advantage of finding Eve near the forbidden tree.

Those who do not want to eat the forbidden fruit should stay away from the forbidden tree.

His purpose in tempting Eve was to use her to tempt Adam. He still sends temptations through people we do not suspect, especially those with the greatest influence over us.

He began by raising a question about whether eating from the tree was really wrong.

He did not reveal his intention at once. His question seemed harmless.

Anyone who wishes to remain safe should be reluctant to engage in conversation with the tempter.

Satan misquoted God's command and spoke mockingly. He has been both a liar and a scoffer from the beginning, and those who mock in the same way show themselves to be his children.

His method is to make God's law seem uncertain or unreasonable, and then lead people into sin.

Our wisdom is to hold firmly to God's commands and honor them highly.

Has God really forbidden lying, misusing his name, drunkenness, and other sins?

Yes, I am sure he has. His commands are right, and by his grace I will keep them.

Eve showed weakness by continuing the conversation. The question itself should have warned her that the serpent meant no good, and she should have turned away.

Satan teaches people first to doubt, and then to deny.

He promised that eating the fruit would benefit them. He wanted them to become dissatisfied with their present condition, as though it were not as good as it could or ought to be.

No outward circumstances will make us content unless our minds learn contentment.

He also tempted them with advancement, as if they were fit to become gods.

Satan had ruined himself by wanting to be like the Most High. Now he wanted to infect our first parents with that same desire and bring them to ruin as well.

He continues to win people over by planting harsh thoughts about God and false hopes of what sin can gain them.

Let us always think of God as the greatest good, and of sin as the greatest evil.

In that way, let us resist the devil, and he will flee from us.

Adam and Eve fall into sin and misery (verses 6–8)

Notice the steps of their transgression. They were not steps upward, but downward toward destruction.

First, Eve saw. Much sin enters through the eyes.

We must not deliberately look at what we are in danger of desiring sinfully (Matthew 5:28).

Second, she took. This was her own action.

Satan can tempt us, but he cannot force us. He may persuade us to throw ourselves down, but he cannot throw us down himself (Matthew 4:6).

Third, she ate. When she first looked, she may not have intended to take the fruit. When she took it, she may not have intended to eat. But that is where it ended.

Wisdom stops sinful desires at their first stirring, before we begin to act on them.

Fourth, she gave the fruit to her husband. Those who do wrong are often willing to draw others into the same wrongdoing.

Fifth, Adam ate. He passed over the tree of life, from which he was free to eat, and chose the forbidden tree of knowledge instead.

In doing so, he showed contempt for what God had given him and a desire for what God had chosen not to give.

He wanted to have whatever pleased him and do whatever pleased him.

In one word, his sin was disobedience (Romans 5:19)—disobedience to a clear, simple, express command.

Adam had no corrupt nature within him to betray him. His freedom of will was still strong, neither weakened nor impaired.

Yet he turned aside so quickly, and brought all his descendants into sin and ruin.

Who can say, then, that Adam's sin did little harm?

Only when it was too late did Adam and Eve see how foolish they had been to eat the forbidden fruit.

They saw the happiness they had lost, the misery into which they had fallen, the loving God they had offended, and the grace and favor they had forfeited.

See what dishonor and trouble sin brings! Wherever it enters, it causes harm and destroys comfort.

Sooner or later, sin brings shame. It will either be the shame of genuine repentance, which ends in glory, or the shame and everlasting contempt to which the wicked will rise on the last day.

People who have sinned often care more about preserving their reputation before others than about receiving pardon from God.

Their excuses are worthless. Like Adam and Eve's fig-leaf coverings, they cannot make the situation any better.

Yet we are all inclined to hide our sins as Adam did.

Before the fall, Adam and Eve would have welcomed God's gracious presence with humble joy. Now his coming terrified them.

No wonder they also became frightened of themselves and overwhelmed with confusion.

The tempter's promise was exposed as a lie. Satan had said they would be safe, but now they could not even feel safe.

Adam and Eve had become miserable comforters to one another.

God calls Adam and Eve to account (verses 9–13)

Listen to God's startling question: “Adam, where are you?”

Those who wander away from God through sin should seriously consider where they are.

They are far from everything good, surrounded by enemies, enslaved to Satan, and on the road to complete ruin.

This lost sheep would have wandered endlessly if the good Shepherd had not searched for him and shown him that he could never be happy or at peace on that path.

If sinners truly considered where they stood, they would not rest until they returned to God.

When people are questioned about wrongdoing, they often admit only what is so obvious that they cannot deny it.

Like Adam, we have good reason to fear approaching God unless we are covered and clothed with the righteousness of Christ.

Sin appears most clearly in the mirror of God's commandment. That is why God placed his command before Adam, and why we should look into it ourselves.

Instead of confessing their sin fully and accepting their shame, Adam and Eve excused themselves and blamed others.

People who give in to temptation have a strange tendency to blame God for tempting them—as though misusing his gifts could excuse breaking his laws.

Those willing to enjoy the pleasure and profit of sin are often unwilling to accept its blame and shame.

Satan's temptations are deceptions. His arguments are lies, and his attractions are traps.

Do not believe him when he speaks pleasantly.

The deceitfulness of sin hardens the heart (Romans 7:11; Hebrews 3:13).

But Satan's cunning cannot excuse our sin. Though he is the tempter, we are the sinners.

Being deceived should not lessen our sorrow for sin. It should deepen our anger at ourselves for allowing a known deceiver and sworn enemy of our souls to mislead us.

The serpent is cursed and the promised Seed is revealed (verses 14–15)

God began his sentence where sin had begun—with the serpent.

The devil's instruments must share in his punishment.

Under the figure of the serpent, the devil was sentenced to be brought low and cursed by God, hated and rejected by humanity, and finally destroyed by the great Redeemer.

The crushing of the serpent's head points to that final defeat.

War was declared between the Seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent.

Because of this hostility, grace and corruption remain in constant conflict within the hearts of God's people.

Satan uses their remaining corruption to strike, sift, and seek to devour them.

Heaven cannot be reconciled with hell, nor light with darkness. Neither can Satan be reconciled with a soul made holy by God.

There is also an ongoing struggle in the world between the wicked and the godly.

Yet here God graciously promised Christ, who would deliver fallen humanity from Satan's power.

The dawn of the gospel had begun. As soon as the wound was inflicted, the remedy was provided and revealed.

This promise of a Savior came without anyone asking or expecting it.

Without a revelation of mercy to give some hope of pardon, a sinner convinced of guilt would sink into despair and become hardened.

Through faith in this promise, our first parents and the patriarchs who lived before the flood were justified and saved.

Three things are revealed here about Christ.

First, his incarnation—his coming in human flesh.

What encouragement it gives sinners to know that their Savior is the woman's Seed, bone of our bone (Hebrews 2:11, 14)!

Second, his sufferings and death, pictured by the serpent bruising his heel—that is, his human nature.

Christ's sufferings also continue in the sufferings of the saints for his name. The devil tempts, persecutes, and kills them, bruising Christ's heel, for Christ is afflicted in their afflictions.

Yet while his heel is bruised on earth, the Head is in heaven.

Third, his victory over Satan through those sufferings.

Christ defeated Satan's temptations and rescued souls from his grasp.

Through his death he struck a fatal blow against the devil's kingdom—a wound to the serpent's head that can never be healed.

As the gospel advances, Satan falls.

The punishment of humanity (verses 16–19)

Because of her sin, the woman was sentenced to sorrow and subjection.

These punishments corresponded to her sin, in which she had sought to satisfy what pleased her eyes and flesh, and to gratify her pride.

Sin brought sorrow into the world and turned it into a valley of tears.

No wonder our sorrows multiply when our sins do too.

The words “He shall rule over you” are God's command: wives are to submit to their husbands.

If the man had not sinned, he would always have ruled with wisdom and love. If the woman had not sinned, she would always have obeyed with humility and gentleness.

Adam blamed his wife. Yet although she was wrong to persuade him to eat the forbidden fruit, he was wrong to listen.

At God's judgment, such empty excuses will turn against those who make them.

God also marked Adam with his displeasure in three ways.

First, his dwelling place was cursed.

God had given the earth to humanity as a pleasant home. Now the ground was cursed because of human sin.

Yet Adam himself was not cursed as the serpent was; the curse fell on the ground for his sake.

Second, his work and its benefits became bitter.

Labor remains our duty, and we must perform it faithfully. It is also part of the sentence placed on humanity, a sentence that idleness defiantly refuses.

The discomfort and exhaustion that accompany work are just punishments. We must bear them patiently, for they are less than our sin deserves.

Even the food produced through our labor becomes less pleasant.

Yet humanity was not sentenced to eat dust like the serpent, but to eat the plants of the field.

Third, human life became short.

Since our days contain so much trouble, their shortness is in one sense a mercy.

Yet death remains dreadful to our nature, even when life itself is unpleasant. So death completes the sentence.

Sin brought death into the world. Had Adam not sinned, he would not have died.

Adam yielded to temptation, but the Savior resisted it.

How wonderfully the satisfaction made by our Lord Jesus through his sufferings and death answers the sentence passed on our first parents!

Did pain in childbirth come through sin? We read of the travail of Christ's soul (Isaiah 53:11), and the pains of death that held him (Acts 2:24).

Did subjection come through sin? Christ was made subject to the law (Galatians 4:4).

Did the curse come through sin? Christ became a curse for us and died a cursed death (Galatians 3:13).

Did thorns come through sin? He was crowned with thorns for us.

Did sweat come through sin? He sweated for us, as though great drops of blood were falling.

Did sorrow come through sin? He was a man of sorrows. In his agony, his soul was overwhelmed with sorrow.

Did death come through sin? He became obedient even to death.

The remedy is as wide as the wound.

Blessed be God for his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ!

God clothes Adam and Eve (verses 20–21)

God named the man Adam, meaning “red earth.” Adam named the woman Eve, meaning “life.”

Adam's name points to the dying body; Eve's name points to the living soul.

Adam probably had the promised Redeemer in mind when he called his wife Eve, or life.

That Redeemer would be the life of all believers, and in him all the families of the earth would be blessed.

See also how God still cared for our first parents despite their sin.

Clothing came into the world with sin.

We have little reason to be proud of our clothes. They are reminders of our shame.

When God made clothes for Adam and Eve, he made them warm, strong, coarse, and plain—not splendid scarlet robes, but garments of skin.

Those who have little to wear should learn not to complain. If they have food and clothing, they can be content; they are as well provided for as Adam and Eve were.

Those who dress richly should learn not to make outward clothing their chief adornment.

It is supposed that the animals whose skins became their clothing were killed not for food, but for sacrifice, as a picture of Christ, the great Sacrifice.

Adam and Eve had made fig-leaf coverings, too narrow to wrap themselves in properly (Isaiah 28:20).

All our own attempts at righteousness are like those inadequate rags.

But God made them garments of skin—large, strong, durable, and suitable.

So it is with the righteousness of Christ.

Therefore, put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

Adam and Eve are driven from Paradise (verses 22–24)

God told the man to leave the garden: he could no longer live there and enjoy it.

But Adam loved the place and was unwilling to go. So God made him leave.

This signified that Adam and all his guilty descendants had been shut out from the fellowship with God that had been the happiness and glory of Paradise.

Yet Adam was sent only to work the ground from which he had been taken.

He was sent to a place of labor, not a place of torment.

Our first parents lost the privileges of their innocent condition, but they were not abandoned to despair.

The way to the tree of life was closed.

From then on, it was useless for Adam or his descendants to expect righteousness, life, and happiness through the covenant of works.

That covenant's command had been broken, and its curse remained fully in force.

If we are judged by that covenant, we are all ruined.

God revealed this to Adam not to drive him to despair, but to stir him to seek life and happiness in the promised Seed.

Through that Seed, a new and living way into God's most holy presence has been opened for us.

Satan assaulted our first parents, to draw them to sin, and the temptation proved fatal to them. The tempter was the devil, in the shape and likeness of a serpent. Satan's plan was to draw our first parents to sin, and so to separate between them and their God. Thus the devil was from the beginning a murderer, and the great mischief maker. The person tempted was the woman: it was Satan's policy to enter into talk with her when she was alone. There are many temptations to which being alone gives great advantage; but the communion of saints tends very much to their strength and safety. Satan took advantage by finding her near the forbidden tree. They that would not eat the forbidden fruit, must not come near the forbidden tree. Satan tempted Eve, that by her he might tempt Adam. It is his policy to send temptations by hands we do not suspect, and by those that have most influence upon us. Satan questioned whether it were a sin or not, to eat of this tree. He did not disclose his design at first, but he put a question which seemed innocent. Those who would be safe, need to be shy of talking with the tempter. He quoted the command wrong. He spoke in a taunting way. The devil, as he is a liar, so he is a scoffer from the beginning; and scoffers are his children. It is the craft of Satan to speak of the Divine law as uncertain or unreasonable, and so to draw people to sin; it is our wisdom to keep up a firm belief of God's command, and a high respect for it. Has God said, Ye shall not lie, nor take his name in vain, nor be drunk, &c.? Yes, I am sure he has, and it is well said; and by his grace I will abide by it. It was Eve's weakness to enter into this talk with the serpent: she might have perceived by his question, that he had no good design, and should therefore have started back. Satan teaches men first to doubt, and then to deny. He promises advantage from their eating this fruit. He aims to make them discontented with their present state, as if it were not so good as it might be, and should be. No condition will of itself bring content, unless the mind be brought to it. He tempts them to seek preferment, as if they were fit to be gods. Satan ruined himself by desiring to be like the Most High, therefore he sought to infect our first parents with the same desire, that he might ruin them too. And still the devil draws people into his interest, by suggesting to them hard thoughts of God, and false hopes of advantage by sin. Let us, therefore, always think well of God as the best good, and think ill of sin as the worst evil: thus let us resist the devil, and he will flee from us.

The woman, for her sin, is condemned to a state of sorrow, and of subjection; proper punishments of that sin, in which she had sought to gratify the desire of her eye, and of the flesh, and her pride. God named the man, and called him Adam, which signifies red earth; Adam named the woman, and called her Eve, that is, life. Adam bears the name of the dying body, Eve of the living soul. He denied what he had done, as if he could hide his crime from God.

He tried to cover a deliberate murder with a deliberate lie.

Murder is a sin that cries out for judgment. Blood calls for blood—the blood of the murdered person calls for the blood of the murderer.

Who can measure the reach or weight of God's curse? How far does it spread? How deeply does it strike?

Only in Christ are believers rescued from that curse and made heirs of blessing.

Cain was cursed from the earth. His punishment came in the very place where he had chosen to set his heart and find his happiness.

Every created thing becomes for us whatever God makes it: a comfort or a burden, a blessing or a curse.

The wicked person's sin brings a curse on what he does and on what he possesses.

Cain complained about his punishment, not his sin.

A heart is terribly hardened when it cares more about suffering than about wrongdoing.

God has wise and holy reasons for allowing even very wicked people to live longer.

It is useless to speculate about what mark God put on Cain.

The mark was certainly recognizable, both as a sign of Cain's disgrace and as God's warning that others must not kill him.

Though Abel died, he still speaks.

He tells us how dreadful murder is. He warns us to suppress anger at its earliest stirrings and teaches that the righteous must expect persecution.

He also points us toward life beyond death and an eternal reward enjoyed through faith in Christ and his atoning sacrifice.

He shows us the excellence of faith in the atoning sacrifice and blood of the Lamb of God.

Cain killed Abel because Cain's deeds were evil and his brother's were righteous (1 John 3:12).

The hostility God announced between the woman's Seed and the serpent's seed had now broken out into open conflict. That struggle has continued ever since.

We are all involved in it. No one can remain neutral.

Our Captain has declared, “Whoever is not with me is against me.”

Let us stand firmly, but with gentleness, for truth and righteousness against Satan.

Cain leaves God's presence (verses 16–18)

Cain cast off all fear of God and no longer attended to his ordinances.

People who pretend to be religious while playing games with God are justly left to themselves until they fall into openly scandalous wrongdoing.

Then they abandon the outward appearance of godliness which their conduct had disgraced, and whose power they had always denied.

Cain went out from the Lord's presence. We never read that he returned to it and found comfort there.

The region where he lived was called Nod. The name can suggest “shaking” or “trembling,” reflecting his restless and unsettled spirit. It can also suggest a land of wandering.

Those who leave God cannot find true rest anywhere else.

People on earth who looked forward to the heavenly city were content to live in tents.

Cain, by contrast, gave no thought to that city and built one here on earth.

So those who remain under God's curse seek their permanent home and satisfaction in this world.

Lamech and the abilities of Cain's descendants (verses 19–24)

The first person recorded as breaking the law of marriage belonged to Cain's wicked family.

Until then, a man had only one wife at a time. Lamech took two.

Worldly people set their hearts on worldly things. They are often very skilled and hardworking in pursuing them.

That was true of Cain's descendants.

Among them was a father of shepherds and a father of musicians—but not a father of the faithful.

There was someone who taught the working of bronze and iron, but no one who taught the good knowledge of the Lord.

They learned how to become rich, powerful, and entertained, but we hear nothing of reverence for God or service to him.

For most people, present things fill their minds.

Lamech had enemies whom he had provoked.

He compared himself with Cain, his ancestor, and flattered himself that his own guilt was much less serious.

He seems to have turned God's patience in sparing Cain into an excuse for expecting to sin without punishment.

Seth and the renewed worship of God (verses 25–26)

The birth of another son comforted Adam and Eve in their sorrow.

They named him Seth, meaning “set,” “settled,” or “placed.”

Through his descendants humanity would continue to the end of time, and from his line the Messiah would come.

Cain, the leader of the departure from God, became a wanderer.

Seth, from whom the true church would come, was established in one place.

Only in Christ and his church can we find a truly lasting home.

Seth followed the example of his murdered brother Abel.

He shared the same precious faith in the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, and became another witness to the grace and power of the Holy Spirit.

God allowed Adam and Eve to see true religion revived within their family.

Those who worshipped God began to do more openly in their faith.

Some publicly professed the true religion, taking a stand against the wickedness of the world around them.

The worse others become, the better and more zealous we should seek to be.

Here began the visible distinction between those who profess God's truth and those who live without reverence for him.

That distinction has continued ever since and will remain as long as the world lasts.

Adam and Seth (verses 1–5)

Adam was made in God's image. But after he fell, he fathered a son in his own likeness—sinful and defiled, weak, miserable, and mortal like himself.

His son was like him not only as a human being with body and soul, but also as a sinner.

This was the opposite of the divine likeness in which Adam had been created. Having lost that likeness, he could not pass it on to his descendants.

Adam lived for 930 years. Then he died, just as God had sentenced him: “You shall return to dust.”

He did not die on the very day he ate the forbidden fruit. But on that day he became mortal, and from then on he began to die.

The rest of his life was a reprieve—a life already forfeited and under sentence of death, slowly wasting away.

Human life is a gradual dying.

The patriarchs from Seth to Enoch (verses 6–20)

Of every one of these patriarchs except Enoch, we read the words, “And he died.”

It is good for us to pay attention to the deaths of others.

These men lived extraordinarily long lives. None died before reaching nearly eight hundred years, and some lived much longer.

That is a very long time for an immortal soul to remain confined within a house of clay.

Life in this world surely did not feel as burdensome to them as it often does now; otherwise they would have grown weary of it.

Nor was the future life revealed to them as clearly as it is to us under the gospel. Otherwise they would have been eager to depart for it.

Every patriarch who lived before the flood, except Noah, was born while Adam was still alive.

They could therefore have learned directly from him about creation, the fall, the promise, and God's commands concerning worship and godly living.

In this way, God preserved the knowledge of his will in his church.

Enoch walks with God (verses 21–24)

Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam.

To be godly is to walk with God. That means being reconciled to him, for two cannot walk together unless they are in agreement (Amos 3:3).

Walking with God includes every part of a godly, righteous, and self-controlled life.

It means keeping God continually before us and acting as people who always live under his gaze.

In everything, we seek to please him and avoid offending him. We follow him as dearly loved children.

Instead of simply saying that Enoch lived, the Holy Spirit says that he walked with God.

This was his constant concern and work.

While other people lived for themselves and for the world, Enoch lived for God. That was the joy of his life.

God took Enoch to a better world.

Because he had not lived like other people, he did not leave the world through death as they did.

He was no longer found, because God had taken him away (Hebrews 11:5).

Enoch had lived only 365 years—little more than half a lifetime compared with the ages of people then.

God often takes earliest those he loves best. The time they lose on earth is more than made up to them in heaven, to their unspeakable benefit.

Notice the way his departure is described: he was no more, because God took him.

He was no longer in this world. He had been changed, as believers still alive at Christ's return will be changed.

Those who begin walking with God when they are young may hope to walk with him for many years, finding comfort and doing good.

A Christian's steady walk in holiness over many years, until God takes that person home, is one of the best recommendations for a faith that many oppose or misuse.

And walking with God fits perfectly well with the responsibilities, comforts, and duties of ordinary life.

Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah (verses 25–32)

Matthew Henry explains Methuselah as meaning something like “when he dies, there is a dart” or “a sending out,” which he connects with the flood that came in the year of Methuselah's death.

Methuselah lived 969 years, longer than any other person on earth.

Yet even the person who lives longest must die at last.

Noah means “rest.” His parents gave him that name in the hope that he would be a great blessing to his generation.

Notice the complaint of Noah's father about the misery of human life since sin entered the world and brought its curse.

Our lives are filled with work, and our time with continual toil.

Because God cursed the ground, even those who work with the greatest care and effort may struggle to earn a bare living from it.

Lamech hoped that Noah's birth would bring relief: “This one will comfort us.”

That expresses the hope parents naturally place in their children—that they will bring them comfort and help. Yet children often turn out differently.

The name also points to a greater expectation.

Do we belong to Christ? Do we have heaven ahead of us?

We need greater comfort in our toil and sorrow than even our closest family or our most promising children can provide.

May we seek and find that comfort in Christ.

The wickedness that provoked God's judgment (verses 1–7)

The most remarkable event in the history of the ancient world was its destruction by the flood.

Here we see how widespread wickedness had become, why God's anger was just, and why he resolved in holiness to punish that world.

Throughout history, God's particular displeasure has rested on marriages between those who profess true faith and those who openly oppose it.

The ungodly spouse's example corrupts the other or seriously weakens that person's faith.

Faith disappears from family life, and children are raised according to the worldly values of the parent who has no fear of God.

If we profess to be sons and daughters of the Lord Almighty, we must not marry without his approval.

He will not bless us when we choose beauty, cleverness, wealth, or worldly honors over faith and holiness.

God's Spirit had been contending with human beings.

He had sent Enoch and Noah, and perhaps others, to preach to them.

He had waited patiently, ready to show grace despite their rebellion. He had also stirred fear and conviction in their consciences.

But the Lord declared that his Spirit would not contend with humanity forever.

He would leave people to become hardened in sin and ready for destruction.

This was because humanity had become flesh: not merely weak and frail, but carnal and corrupt.

People had misused the noble powers of their souls to satisfy sinful desires.

God sees all the wickedness among human beings.

Nothing can be hidden from him now. And unless people repent, he will soon bring what they have done into the open.

A nation's wickedness is especially great when notorious sinners are celebrated as famous people.

Sin was being committed everywhere, by every kind of person.

Anyone could see that humanity's wickedness was great.

But God saw something deeper: every thought and intention of the human heart was continually evil.

Here lay the bitter root and the polluted spring.

The heart was deceitful and desperately wicked. Its principles were corrupt, its habits and desires evil.

People planned evil and deliberately worked out ways to cause harm.

No goodness remained among them.

God looked upon their wickedness as one who had himself been injured by it.

He saw it as a loving father sees the folly and stubborn rebellion of a disobedient child—a grief so deep that the father might wish he had never had that child.

Scripture speaks here in human terms.

It does not mean that God can change or become unhappy.

If God hates our sin so deeply, should we not grieve over it ourselves?

May we look upon the One we have grieved and mourn!

God regretted having made humanity. Yet Scripture never says that he regretted redeeming humanity.

When God resolved to destroy human beings, the original expression was especially striking: “I will wipe humanity from the earth.”

The image is of dirt being wiped from a place that should be clean and thrown onto a refuse heap.

Even as God pronounced judgment, he spoke of humanity as his own creation.

Those who fail to fulfill the purpose for which life was given forfeit their lives.

God made this decision only after his Spirit had contended with people for so long without success.

God's justice punishes only those who refuse to be reformed by his grace.

Noah finds grace (verses 8–11)

Noah did not find favor with other people.

They hated and persecuted him, because his life and preaching condemned the world around him.

But he found grace in the Lord's eyes.

That made him far more honorable than the celebrated people of his age.

Let this be our deepest desire: to live in a way that is pleasing to God.

While the rest of the world lived wickedly, Noah kept his integrity.

It was God's favor toward Noah that produced this good life in him.

Noah was a righteous man, justified before God through faith in the promised Seed.

Through that faith he was made holy, received right principles, and lived uprightly among others.

He was not simply honest. He was devoted to God, continually seeking to do his will.

God looks with favor upon those who sincerely look up to him in faith.

It is easy to seem religious when religion is fashionable.

But it takes strong faith and determination to go against the current and stand for God when no one else will.

That is what Noah did.

Every kind of sin was found among the people. They corrupted God's worship.

Sin had filled the earth with violence, fully justifying God's decision to destroy the world.

The corruption spread everywhere.

When wickedness becomes widespread, ruin is not far away.

As long as a nation has a remnant of people who pray, their intercession may keep judgment back even as the nation's guilt continues to grow.

But when everyone is breaking down the barriers through sin, and no one stands in the breach to repair them, what can we expect but a flood of wrath?

The coming flood and the building of the ark (verses 12–21)

God told Noah that he intended to destroy the wicked world with water.

“The Lord confides in those who fear him” (Psalm 25:14).

His secret is shared with all believers, enabling them to understand and apply the warnings and promises of his written word.

God chose a flood to drown the world.

Just as he chooses the rod with which to correct his children, he chooses the sword with which to destroy his enemies.

God established his covenant with Noah.

This is the first place in the Bible where the word covenant appears.

Here it seems to refer to two things.

First, the covenant of providence: the ordinary course of nature would continue to the end of time.

Second, the covenant of grace: God would be Noah's God and would take a people for himself from Noah's descendants.

God then directed Noah to build an ark.

It was something like the hull of a ship, built to float on the water.

The ark was enormous. Henry compares its size to half that of St. Paul's Cathedral and says it could hold more than eighteen of the largest ships of his day.

God could have kept Noah safe without making him work or endure any expense or difficulty.

Instead, he gave Noah the task of making the very means by which he would be preserved.

This tested Noah's faith and obedience.

Both God's providence and his grace recognize and reward obedience and diligence.

God gave Noah detailed instructions for the ark. Built according to those instructions, it was perfectly suited to its purpose.

God promised to preserve Noah and his family in it.

When we obey God, both we and our families are likely to benefit.

The godliness of parents benefits their children in this life and helps them toward eternal life, provided they make proper use of those blessings.

Noah's faith and obedience (verse 22)

Noah's faith overcame every objection raised by unbelieving reasoning.

He had to build an enormous structure unlike anything he had ever seen, and provide food for all the living creatures it would shelter.

That demanded great care, labor, and expense.

His neighbors would surely laugh at him.

Yet by faith Noah overcame every objection. He obeyed promptly and firmly.

Once he began building, he did not stop until the ark was finished.

That is what he did, and what we must do.

He feared the coming flood, and so he prepared the ark.

Noah's warning also contains an even more solemn warning for us: we must flee from the wrath to come.

That judgment will sweep the unbelieving world into the pit of destruction.

Christ is the true Noah, the One who brings us comfort.

Through his sufferings he has already prepared the ark of salvation, and he graciously invites us to enter it by faith.

While the day of his patience continues, let us hear his voice and obey him.

Noah was counted righteous not because of any righteousness of his own, but because he was an heir of the righteousness that comes through faith (Hebrews 11:7).

He believed God's revelation of a Savior and sought and expected salvation through him alone. Thus he was justified by faith and received the Spirit, whose fruit is every kind of goodness. Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.

Only one week remained—one more Sabbath in which to consider what would bring them peace.

Those who have neglected their souls through long years of health, treating death as something far away, often remain just as careless during their last days of sickness, even when death is close. Their hearts have been hardened by sin's deceitfulness.

By faith in God's warning, Noah prepared the ark because a flood was coming. By that same faith, he entered the ark when God warned him that the flood would come very soon.

On the very day Noah was safely settled inside, the fountains of the great deep burst open.

The earth contained waters which, at God's command, sprang up and flooded it. Similarly, our bodies contain fluids that, when God permits, can become the sources of deadly diseases.

The windows of heaven opened too, pouring onto the earth the waters above the firmament—that is, in the air.

Ordinary rain falls in drops. But the rain that came then was unlike any rain before or since. For forty days and nights it fell without stopping or easing, over the whole earth at once.

God exercised his almighty power in a special way to bring about the flood. It is therefore useless and presumptuous to think that human wisdom can fully explain how he did it.

Even fierce and dangerous animals became gentle and manageable in the ark. Yet when that occasion passed, they remained the same kinds of creatures as before. Being in the ark had not changed their natures.

So it is with hypocrites in the church. They may outwardly conform to the rules of that ark, but their hearts remain unchanged. Sooner or later their true character will appear.

God continued to care for Noah. He shut the door to keep Noah safe inside and to keep everyone else outside for good. God has not told us exactly how he shut it.

Our great duty, in obedience to the gospel call, is to enter by living faith in Christ the way of salvation God has prepared for sinners.

Those who enter the ark should seek to bring as many others as possible, through sound teaching, loving persuasion, and good example. There is room in Christ for everyone who comes.

What means death leading to death for unbelievers becomes life leading to life for the faithful.

No one has the right to take their own life. Our lives belong to God, and we must surrender them only when he decides.

If we do anything to hasten our own death, we are accountable to him.

When God demands an account of a life unjustly taken, the murderer cannot give that life back and must answer with his own.

Sooner or later, in this world or the next, God will expose murders and punish those that are beyond human justice.

Yet God has appointed authorities to protect the innocent and restrain wrongdoers. They must not carry the sword in vain (Romans 13:4).

Henry insists that deliberate murder should be punished by death.

The reason given for the seriousness of murder is that even fallen humanity still bears traces of God's image. Unjustly killing a human being therefore defaces that image and dishonors God.

God's covenant and the rainbow (verses 8–17)

The old world was destroyed as a testimony to divine justice. The continued existence of this world is a testimony to divine mercy.

Yet the sin that drowned the old world will one day bring this one to destruction by fire.

People seal agreements to make their promises solemn and give one another assurance that they will be kept.

God appointed the rainbow as the seal of his covenant.

It seems likely that rainbows had appeared in clouds before the flood. But they had never been a sign of this covenant until God made them so.

A rainbow appears when we have the greatest reason to fear that the rain will overwhelm us.

At that very moment, God displays the sign of his promise that it will not prevail.

The darker the cloud, the brighter the bow shining within it.

In the same way, when threatening troubles multiply, God's encouragements can abound even more.

A rainbow is formed when sunlight shines upon or through drops of rain.

Likewise, all the glory belonging to the seals of God's covenant comes from Christ, the Sun of righteousness. He can shine with glory even upon the tears of his people.

An ordinary bow can inspire fear. But this bow has neither string nor arrow.

It cannot hurt us. It points upward rather than toward the earth.

God meant the signs of his covenant to comfort us, not terrify us.

As God looks upon the rainbow and remembers his covenant, we should look upon it with faith and thankfulness and remember that same covenant.

Without God's revelation, we could never know this gracious assurance. Without faith, that assurance would bring us no benefit.

The same is true of the greater dangers facing humanity and the blessings promised under the new covenant.

Noah's drunkenness and his sons' conduct (verses 18–23)

Scripture records Noah's drunkenness with a fairness and honesty found only in the Bible.

It shows the weakness and imperfection of even a good man—though he may have fallen into this sin unexpectedly.

The best people cannot stand upright unless they depend on God's grace and are upheld by it.

Ham appears to have been a bad man. He probably took pleasure in seeing his father in such a shameful condition.

Noah had been described as blameless among the people of his generation (Genesis 6:9). That meant sincere faithfulness, not sinless perfection.

He had remained sober while surrounded by drunken people. Now he became drunk in a setting where the people around him were sober.

Whoever thinks he stands should be careful not to fall.

When we enjoy God's good gifts in abundance, we must be particularly careful not to misuse them through excess (Luke 21:34).

Noah's sin brought shame. Drunkenness is a serious evil.

It exposes people's weaknesses and reveals secrets they would otherwise keep hidden. A drunken gatekeeper leaves the gates open.

It also disgraces people and exposes them to contempt. Those who are drunk say and do things they would be ashamed even to think of when sober.

Notice the care Shem and Japheth took to cover their father's shame.

Love should cover the faults of others (1 Peter 4:8).

And parents and others deserving our respect should be treated with an additional covering of reverence.

God's blessing rests upon those who honor their parents, while his curse especially falls upon those who dishonor them.

Noah speaks about Canaan, Shem, and Japheth (verses 24–29)

Noah pronounced a curse upon Canaan, Ham's son. Perhaps Canaan had been more guilty than the others.

He was to become a servant of servants—the lowest and most despised of servants—even to his brothers.

Henry connects this prophecy with Israel's later victories over the Canaanites, when they were killed in battle or compelled to pay tribute.

He also describes Africa as having been populated largely by Ham's descendants and interprets the continent's history through that framework.

He points to periods of Roman, Saracen, and Turkish domination, and describes the ignorance, violence, enslavement, and misery he believed were widespread in parts of Africa during his own period.

He grieves that so many Black Africans were bought and sold like animals in the marketplace, transported far from their homes, and forced to perform exhausting labor.

But he expressly refuses to use these events as an excuse for those who profit from such cruelty.

God has never commanded people to enslave Black Africans. Henry declares that God will certainly punish those who commit such terrible wrongs.

Henry regarded the course of history as a fulfillment of Noah's prophecy. He argued that it showed Noah was not simply speaking out of personal anger, but that the Holy Spirit had used Ham's offense to reveal God's hidden purposes.

“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem.”

Henry understands the church as being preserved among Shem's descendants. From them came the Jewish people, who for a long time were the only people publicly professing faith in the true God.

Christ, who is the Lord God, would also descend from Shem in his human nature.

Noah blessed Japheth too, and with him the nations descended from his family across the islands and distant lands.

This points to the conversion of the Gentiles and their entrance into the church.

Henry explains that the blessing may be read as saying that God would persuade Japheth, who would then dwell in Shem's tents.

Jew and Gentile would be united in the gospel fold. Both would become one in Christ.

Noah lived long enough to see two worlds: the world before the flood and the world after it.

Yet as an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith, he now rests in hope, waiting to see a world better than either.

The seal of this covenant was the rainbow, which, it is likely, was seen in the clouds before, but was never a seal of the covenant till now it was made so. Ham appears to have been a bad man, and probably rejoiced to find his father in an unbecoming situation. It was said of Noah, that he was perfect in his generations, ch. 6:9; but this is meant of sincerity, not of a sinless perfection. Men say and do that when drunken, which, when sober, they would blush to think of. Notice the care of Shem and Japheth to cover their father's shame. There is a mantle of love to be thrown over the faults of all, [1Pet.4.8] 1Pe 4:8. Beside that, there is a robe of reverence to be thrown over the faults of parents and other superiors. The blessing of God attends on those who honour their parents, and his curse lights especially on those who dishonour them.

Noah declares a curse on Canaan, the son of Ham; perhaps this grandson of his was more guilty than the rest. A servant of servants, that is, The meanest and most despicable servant, shall he be, even to his brethren. This certainly points at the victories in after-times obtained by Israel over the Canaanites, by which they were put to the sword, or brought to pay tribute. The whole continent of Africa was peopled mostly by the descendants of Ham; and for how many ages have the better parts of that country lain under the dominion of the Romans, then of the Saracens, and now of the Turks! Nimrod, a mighty hunter, ruler, and builder (verses 8–14)

Nimrod became a powerful man in his day.

Before him, people had generally been content to live on equal terms with their neighbors. Each man ruled his own household, but no one claimed authority over other households.

Nimrod wanted to dominate his neighbors.

The spirit of the giants before the flood—those mighty and famous men (Genesis 6:4)—came to life again in him.

Nimrod was a mighty hunter.

Hunting was then a way to prevent wild animals from multiplying until they became dangerous.

It demanded courage and skill. As a result, Nimrod gained opportunities to command others and gradually gathered many people under his leadership.

It was probably through this activity that he first acquired power and began forcing others to submit to him.

He violated his neighbors' rights and property, persecuted innocent people, and sought to make everything his own through force and violence.

He continued his oppression in defiance of God himself.

Nimrod was also a powerful ruler.

Through some combination of strategy and military force, he established a monarchy that terrified the powerful and seemed likely to dominate the whole world.

He was a great builder too.

Notice what his life teaches us about ambition.

Ambition has no limits. The more it has, the more it wants. It is always crying, “Give me more!”

Ambition cannot rest. Once Nimrod ruled four cities, he was not content until he had four more.

Ambition is costly. Nimrod would rather bear the enormous expense of building cities than miss the honor of ruling them.

Ambition is reckless. It will stop at nothing.

Nimrod's name signifies rebellion. Tyrants over other people are rebels against God.

A day is coming when conquerors will no longer receive the praise they are given in the partial histories written by human beings.

In the impartial record of Scripture, they will instead be remembered with disgrace.

Canaan's descendants were numerous and prosperous. Their land was rich and pleasantly situated.

Yet Canaan was under God's curse—and that curse was not without a cause.

Those under God's curse may prosper for a time in this world.

We cannot determine whether a person lives under God's love or his displeasure merely by looking at outward circumstances.

The decisive question concerns what is happening within.

God's curse always acts, and its consequences are terrible.

It may work secretly, affecting the soul without anything visible to others.

Or it may work slowly, without immediate consequences. But it reserves unrepentant sinners for a day of wrath.

Canaan had a more desirable land than either Shem or Japheth.

Yet Shem and Japheth had a better inheritance: the blessing of God.

Abram and his descendants, God's covenant people, came through Eber. From Eber they received the name Hebrews.

How much better it is to become like Eber, the father of a family of faithful and upright people, than to become the father of a family driven by the pursuit of power, worldly riches, or empty pleasures!

Goodness is true greatness.
